purpose: The mechanical command boundaries, in one place. hooks/guard.py enforces them for commands Claude runs through the Bash tool; scripts/delegate enforces them inside a delegated OpenCode run, where the hook cannot see anything. Both read this file and each translates it into its own matching form - token parsing in the hook, glob patterns in the dispatcher's permission policy. Nothing here is written in either engine's syntax, and neither engine keeps its own copy of a rule.
how_to_change: Add or edit a rule here, not in a consumer. tests/test_parser.py fails by rule name when a rule is not enforced by both consumers that declare a decision for it, when its documented_in heading is missing from the skill it names, or when an example is not caught. Rule order is precedence: the first match wins.

decisions.hook: What hooks/guard.py decides for a command Claude runs. null means this rule is not the hook's to enforce.
decisions.delegated: What scripts/delegate's permission policy decides inside a delegated run. null means the rule cannot be expressed there, or does not apply.
decisions.not_enforced_because: Required whenever hook or delegated is null. A rule that no longer applies to a consumer has to say why, in the data, where the next reader sees it. Without this field a decision could be quietly dropped to null and nothing would notice - which is the shape of the divergence this file exists to prevent, not a hypothetical.

match_kinds.program_subcommand: program name, plus the subcommand that follows it, options skipped
match_kinds.program_option: program name, plus an option appearing anywhere in the command
match_kinds.segment_text: an identifier appearing anywhere in the command text, including inside a quoted snippet or a heredoc body

rules.name: push
rules.intent: Pushing is never automatic. It leaves the machine, and there is no human inside a delegated run to ask.

rules.name: blanket-staging
rules.intent: Staging everything sweeps in unrelated work. Stage the files the task created or changed, by path.

rules.name: commit-inside-delegated-run
rules.intent: The orchestrator creates the commit after review passes. An implementer that commits mid-run bypasses diff inspection and the cleanup checklist. Claude's own commits are the normal path, so the hook does not enforce this.

not_enforced_because.hook: Claude commits as the normal end of a task, after review passes. The rule is about an implementer committing mid-run, and only a delegated run can do that.

rules.name: discard-tracked-changes
rules.intent: `git reset --hard` throws away every uncommitted change in the tree, including work this task never touched, and unstaged work leaves no reflog entry to recover from. --merge and --keep discard the same way on a dirty tree. The index-only forms are left alone: `git reset`, `--soft` and `--mixed` move HEAD or unstage, and the file contents survive.

rules.name: discard-pathspec-changes
rules.intent: `git checkout -- <path>` and `git checkout .` overwrite working-tree files from the index or a commit. There is no reflog for unstaged content, so whatever the user had uncommitted in those paths is gone. Branch operations are untouched: the rule fires on the pathspec forms only. A bare `git checkout <path>` with no `--` is not caught, because at this layer it is indistinguishable from a branch name.

rules.name: discard-worktree
rules.intent: `git restore` overwrites working-tree files from the index by default, and `git clean` deletes untracked files outright - the one category Git itself cannot give back. Every form is covered rather than only the forced ones: `git clean -n` and `--dry-run` are safe, but `git status --porcelain` answers the same question, and a decision that the hook applies and the delegated policy cannot is the divergence this file exists to prevent. `git restore --staged` is included for the same reason.

rules.name: drop-stash
rules.intent: `git stash clear` and `git stash drop` delete stash entries permanently - and a dropped stash is exactly where the user's interrupted work was put for safekeeping. Creating a stash is not covered: `git stash` and `git stash push` move changes out of the tree but preserve them, and `git stash pop` puts them back, so they are disruptive rather than destructive.

rules.name: force-branch-ref
rules.intent: `git branch -D` deletes a branch Git has established is not merged anywhere, and `-f`/`--force`/`-M` move an existing branch ref onto a different commit. Both abandon commits that nothing else points at. Reading and listing branches is untouched, and so is `git branch -d`, which Git already refuses when the branch would be lost.

rules.name: expire-recovery-refs
rules.intent: The reflog is what makes a bad reset survivable. `git reflog expire`, `git reflog delete` and `git gc --prune=now` drop it and the unreachable objects it points at, which turns a recoverable mistake into a permanent one - and they are most tempting immediately after the mistake. Reading the reflog and ordinary housekeeping are untouched.

rules.name: rewrite-repository-history
rules.intent: `git filter-branch` and `git filter-repo` rewrite every commit they are pointed at, and `git update-ref` writes or deletes a ref directly with none of the safety a porcelain command applies. None of the three has a read-only form - `git log`, `git rev-parse` and `git show-ref` read the same data without touching it.

rules.name: rebase-inside-delegated-run
rules.intent: A rebase rewrites the commits on the branch it was handed. Claude rebases with the user present and the reflog behind it, so the hook leaves it alone; a delegated implementer has no reason to reach for one, and nothing is watching the branch it rewrites.

not_enforced_because.hook: Claude rebases as an ordinary local operation, with the user present and the reflog available to undo it. The boundary that matters here is the unattended one, which only a delegated run crosses.

rules.name: recursive-delete
rules.intent: Recursion is what turns deleting a file into deleting a tree: `rm -rf .` and `rm -rf <dir>` take everything below the path, tracked or not, with no Git copy of untracked content to restore from. Deleting a named file is left alone - an implementation task legitimately removes a file it was asked to remove. Both matchers compare whole tokens, so the option spellings are enumerated here rather than decomposed; an unlisted cluster is a gap in this rule, not a decision.

rules.name: mass-delete
rules.intent: `find ... -delete` removes every path the traversal matched, and the traversal is usually wider than the author pictured. The same search without -delete prints what it found, which is the step that should come first.

rules.name: overwrite-file-contents
rules.intent: shred, truncate and dd exist to overwrite bytes in place. There is no staging step and no Git copy of an untracked file, so a wrong path is unrecoverable, and none of the three is a normal tool for editing source. Matching is by program name, so a command whose name merely starts with one of these - ddrescue, for instance - is caught too; that is stated here rather than discovered later.

rules.name: site-named
rules.intent: A bench command carrying --site runs against that live site's database or a running Frappe instance. Confirm the single target site first.

rules.name: site-unnamed
rules.intent: These bench subcommands act on a site, and with no --site they do not stop acting on one: frappe resolves it from default_site, then currentsite.txt. The site acted on is whichever the bench was last pointed at, named nowhere. 75 of these are derived from frappe's own CLI - every command in frappe/commands/*.py that resolves a site - rather than filtered by which look dangerous; re-derive them the same way against a newer frappe instead of appending by hand. "run" is the 76th, retained from this rule's earlier four-entry form; frappe's current CLI has no such command.

rules.name: database-client
rules.intent: A direct route to the database, bypassing every Frappe-shaped rule around it.

rules.name: frappe-connection
rules.intent: A snippet that opens a Frappe connection reaches a site without naming a bench command. Not expressible as a command pattern in a delegated run, where the site rules above cover the same ground. Rule order is precedence, and a bench command carrying a snippet is caught by the bench rules above first - both ask, so the outcome is the same.

not_enforced_because.delegated: Not expressible as a command pattern: it matches an identifier anywhere in the command text, including inside a quoted snippet. The bench and database-client rules deny the delegated routes to the same place.

rules.name: bare-agent-run
rules.intent: A coding agent started outside the dispatcher carries none of the central routing, none of this permission policy, and no result contract. The dispatcher launches the CLIs as its own child processes, which are not Bash tool calls, so it is not caught by its own rule.

not_enforced_because.delegated: A delegated run is already inside the dispatcher. Nesting is not the boundary this rule protects.

rules.name: bare-agent-exec
rules.intent: The same rule for the other agent CLI. Separate because each CLI has its own subcommand and its own options that take a separate argument.
